intro.heading: Nothing happened. That is exactly why it is easy to forget.
intro.sub: A scenario we see in many care settings.
intro.paragraph: A senior carer is doing the morning medication round when she notices a dose that was almost given at the wrong time. She stops, checks and puts it right. Nobody is harmed. She tells the manager, who records it in the home's usual way. Everyone feels relieved and a little uneasy. The manager does not want a formal meeting that makes people feel accused, but a quiet word with two people will not reach the whole team either. The close call is logged. The learning has nowhere to go. Here is how that plays out.

trail.text: A carer stops herself before a dose goes out at the wrong time.
She tells the senior and the dose is put right. No harm done.
The manager records the close call in the way the home always does.
The manager wants the team to learn from it without anyone feeling blamed.
A team meeting feels heavy. A quiet word only reaches two people.
Nobody knows who else is unsure about the same step.
A new carer is shown the round. The close call is a line in a log.
“What did you learn from your close calls?” A list is not an answer.

trail_close: The close call was handled well. The learning is the gap. Here is how CareStream helps with the part that comes after the record, without replacing how you report.

why.heading: A log shows what happened. It does not show what the team now knows.
why.sub: Learning from mistakes works best when it feels safe, quick and specific.

cards.title: A blame meeting teaches people to stay quiet
cards.body: If speaking up leads to a formal sit down, people think twice next time. A short, private check on the topic keeps the focus on the point, not the person.

cards.title: One word does not reach everyone
cards.body: The two people involved know what happened. Others on different shifts may share the same doubt and never hear about it.

cards.title: Writing a refresher by hand takes time
cards.body: Few managers can write a fresh module after each close call, so the learning stays a line in a log and the same slip can come back.

talk.heading: The questions managers ask, and how CareStream answers them
talk.sub: Read this as a conversation. The questions are the ones we hear most.

items.q: Does CareStream replace how we record a close call?
items.a: No. CareStream does not hold your incident records or log events. You record the event wherever you do now, in your own system or on paper. CareStream is for the learning that follows, once the record is made.

items.q: How do I use it after a close call on the medication round?
items.a: Open the Training screen and allocate an adhoc module on the topic, medication for example. It is built from your own policies where they cover it, with general good practice as the fallback. You can edit and preview it, tick the staff, and set a due date if you want one.

items.q: How is this different from a team meeting about it?
items.a: Each carer answers a few questions privately on their own phone, so nobody is put on the spot in front of colleagues. It reaches people on every shift, not just those who were there. A wrong answer is information about a gap, not a mark against a person.

items.q: What happens when someone gets a question wrong?
items.a: The wrong answer goes into that carer's Follow-up tab in the Staff Hub, and they get an email, at most once a day. They choose Learn & retry, a short lesson then a fresh question, or Just retry the same question. They can retry as often as they like.

items.q: Will I be told every time someone gets one wrong?
items.a: No, and that is deliberate. Nothing alerts you on each wrong answer. You see the picture in the Knowledge gaps view in Analytics and in the Monday digest email. That keeps the tone calm and shows you patterns, not individual slips.

items.q: What if our policy does not cover the point?
items.a: Then the module falls back on general good practice. That is a useful prompt. If a close call shows your policy is thin, you can look at the gap and decide whether to improve the policy. The examples in any mock up are illustration only, not clinical advice.

items.q: Can staff who speak another first language follow it?
items.a: Yes. They can open the lesson in their own language, so a wrong answer points to a gap in knowledge and not in vocabulary. Translation is on the paid plans only, and the reminder emails are in English.

items.q: Can I try it on a real close call?
items.a: Yes. There is a 14 day free trial, and you can create a free account to look around. The adhoc training screen is part of the paid plans, so check the pricing page for what each plan includes.

limits.heading: The learning that follows, not the report itself

cards.title: It is not a place to log the event
cards.body: There is no way to log the event in CareStream. You keep recording wherever you do now, and use CareStream for the training that follows.

cards.title: It does not investigate or give clinical advice
cards.body: It does not find the cause of a close call or decide what went wrong. That is a manager's judgement, and your own procedures and clinicians still lead.

cards.title: It does not alert you to every wrong answer
cards.body: You see the picture in Knowledge gaps and the Monday digest. Adhoc training and translation are on the paid plans, and a close call does not trigger anything automatically.

items.q: What counts as a close call in a care home?
items.a: It is an event that could have caused harm but did not, because someone caught it or luck intervened. A dose nearly given at the wrong time, caught before it reached the resident, is a typical example. Your own policy should say how your home defines and records them.

items.q: Do I have to report a close call under RIDDOR?
items.a: RIDDOR covers certain dangerous occurrences, which HSE describes as incidents with the potential to cause harm. Whether a particular event is reportable depends on the rules, so check the HSE guidance. Our post on RIDDOR reporting in care homes explains more.

items.q: What is near miss reporting, and does CareStream do it?
items.a: Close call reporting means recording events that nearly caused harm, so patterns can be seen. CareStream does not do it. Use the way your home already records them, then use CareStream for the follow up training.

items.q: Why does learning from incidents matter if nobody was hurt?
items.a: A close call shows where the system was one step from harm. Learning from incidents at this point costs nothing but time, and it can stop the same slip becoming an injury.

items.q: How do I get incident learning to reach every shift?
items.a: Allocate a short module to the whole team, not just the people involved. Each person completes it on their own phone when they are next on shift, and the Knowledge gaps view shows where it landed.

items.q: Is this the same as adhoc training?
items.a: Yes. Adhoc training is a short module you allocate when something happens. Here the trigger is a close call. The adhoc training page covers the wider idea, and this page is about keeping it blame free.

items.q: How do I make learning from mistakes feel safe for staff?
items.a: Say why you are doing it, and send it to everyone, not only those involved. Keep the questions about the topic, not the event. A wrong answer opens a short lesson, which treats it as a gap to fill. The incident led training post has more on tone.

items.q: What if a carer gets a question wrong?
items.a: It appears in their Follow-up tab. They can choose Learn & retry, a short lesson on that point followed by a fresh question, or Just retry the same question, as often as they need.

items.q: Can it help with medication specifically?
items.a: You can allocate a medication module and see which questions are missed. It does not replace competency checks. Our medication course covers the topic itself, and a competent person still observes practice.

guide.heading: A practical way to learn from a close call
guide.lede: A close call is the cheapest lesson a home ever gets. The skill is turning it into learning that is quick, kind and reaches everyone.

sections.h3: Keep the record and the learning apart
paragraphs: Record the event first, in the way your home always does. That record is your evidence of what happened and what you did. The learning is a separate, lighter step. Keeping them apart helps staff see that a short module is about the topic, not about blame.

Good governance expects services to assess and mitigate risk. Regulation 12 of the 2014 regulations includes assessing risks to people's health and safety, mitigating them, the proper and safe management of medicines, and staff having the competence and skills to do so safely. A close call on the medication round touches all of those.

sections.h3: Four steps that fit a busy day
checklist: Same day: record the close call where you already do, and thank the person who spoke up.
Within a few days: allocate a short module on the topic to the whole team, built from your policies.
Whenever an answer is wrong: the carer opens a short lesson on that point, then a fresh question.
Each month: look at the most missed questions and decide whether the policy, the training or the process needs a change.

sections.h3: What to say to the team
paragraphs: Tell people plainly why the module is coming. Something like: we had a close call, nobody was hurt, and we all want to be sure we are clear on this step. Say that wrong answers are normal and that the lesson is the point. Staff who feel safe will report the next close call sooner.

guide.note: For the inspector. Keep the close call record, the module you allocated and the results together, so you can show what you did next as well as what happened.
